title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 8: Destiny and Legacy, Not Dynasty
keywords: the darling of the world again
a moratorium of say three years
primary_topics: Chapter 8 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 6) -- CJP's May 30, 2010 Inquirer column arguing that what propelled Noynoy Aquino was 'destiny and legacy, not dynasty,' as Time Magazine had suggested, and how the 'tsunami of votes' could be leveraged against corruption and poverty

The international goodwill the landslide generated -- congratulations from ambassadors before canvassing even began and two Time features in under a month, making the country 'the darling of the world again' -- and how it could draw investments, grants and favorable trade terms

His concrete economic proposal -- using the goodwill to negotiate 'sovereign debt waivers' or at least a 'three-year moratorium' on international-debt amortizations, freeing 'meager funds' for 'pump-priming and job creation'

The emotional core -- Ninoy Aquino's August 25, 1973 prison letter to the teenage Noynoy (shared by retired Justice Flerida Ruth Romero), which CJP reads as the source of Noynoy's 'passion to liberate his people,' bequeathing the family name and the charge to 'live with honor and follow your conscience'
sub_topics: The mandate restated: the people gave Noynoy 'the most overwhelming mandate since our present Constitution took effect in 1987,' choosing peaceful transition by 'rolling a tsunami of votes' rather than 'mammoth street rallies' -- 'a new form of People Power'

International goodwill: the triumph 'so impressed the international community' that ambassadors of the United States (Harry Thomas Jr.), China (Liu Jianchao), Japan (Makoto Katsura) and the EU (Alistair MacDonald) congratulated Noynoy 'even before... canvassing had begun,' while Time featured him twice in under a month, making the Philippines 'the darling of the world again'

Leveraging the moment: this 'shining moment' should be used 'in the war against corruption and poverty,' since the goodwill 'can generate new investments, funding grants (like from the US Millennium Challenge Corporation), and favorable trade agreements'

The debt proposal: with 'innovation and imagination,' Noynoy could negotiate 'sovereign debt waivers' (principal or interest) or 'at the very least, a moratorium of say three years' on international-debt amortizations -- giving him 'the capacity to meet immediate... expectations' while diverting funds to 'pump-priming and job creation'

The letter's origin: asking what gave Noynoy his 'passion to liberate his people from corruption and poverty,' CJP turns to Ninoy's August 25, 1973 prison letter (a copy from retired Justice Flerida Ruth Romero), written under martial law as Ninoy explained -- after consulting lawyers Salonga and Tañada -- his refusal to take part in the 'one-sided' Military Commission, expecting life imprisonment or a firing squad

The act of conscience: Ninoy cast his refusal as 'an act of conscience' and a 'protest against the structures of injustice,' a 'last act of defiance against tyranny and dictatorship,' even as he regretted being unable to secure his children's future

The bequest: unable to leave wealth, Ninoy wrote that the one 'valuable asset' he could bequeath was the family name, kept 'untarnished,' and apologized for placing 'the great responsibility for our family' on his son's 'young shoulders,' urging him to stand by his mother and inherit her 'indomitable spirit and... silent courage'

Destiny, not dynasty: Ninoy's parting charge was to 'live with honor and follow your conscience' and serve the nation, telling his son 'the ball is now in your hands'; like Cory, Noynoy 'had no plans of seeking the presidency' until his mother's August 1, 2009 death 'altered history' -- so, contrary to Time's 'dynasty,' CJP credits destiny and legacy for kindling Noynoy's 'passion to liberate his people'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 6), CJP's May 30, 2010 Inquirer column, argues that what propelled Noynoy Aquino was 'destiny and legacy, not dynasty' -- Time Magazine's word -- and shows how the 'tsunami of votes' could be turned against corruption and poverty. The landslide 'so impressed the international community' that ambassadors of the US (Harry Thomas Jr.), China (Liu Jianchao), Japan (Makoto Katsura) and the EU (Alistair MacDonald) congratulated Noynoy 'even before... canvassing had begun,' and Time featured him twice in under a month, making the Philippines 'the darling of the world again.' This 'shining moment,' CJP urges, should be leveraged to draw 'new investments, funding grants (like from the US Millennium Challenge Corporation), and favorable trade agreements' -- and, concretely, to negotiate 'sovereign debt waivers' or 'at the very least, a moratorium of say three years' on international-debt amortizations, freeing 'meager funds' for 'pump-priming and job creation.' For the source of Noynoy's 'passion to liberate his people,' CJP turns to Ninoy Aquino's August 25, 1973 prison letter (shared by retired Justice Flerida Ruth Romero), written under martial law to explain -- after consulting Salonga and Tañada -- his refusal to join the 'one-sided' Military Commission, an 'act of conscience' and 'protest against the structures of injustice' by which he 'decided to walk into the very jaws of death.' Unable to leave wealth, Ninoy bequeathed the family name kept 'untarnished,' apologized for the 'great responsibility' on his son's 'young shoulders,' and urged him to stand by his mother and inherit her 'indomitable spirit and... silent courage,' closing: 'live with honor and follow your conscience... the ball is now in your hands.' Like Cory, Noynoy 'had no plans of seeking the presidency' until his mother's August 1, 2009 death 'altered history' -- so, against the 'dynasty' label, CJP credits destiny and legacy.
